name: Turkesterone
lead: Turkesterone is a phytoecdysteroid, a plant steroid related to the molting hormones of insects, found in Ajuga turkestanica and in Vitex species, Cyanotis arachnoidea, wheat and Rhaponticum acaule [1][2][26]. It is sold as an oral dietary supplement and promoted to lifters and bodybuilders as a natural route to more muscle size, strength and recovery, which in turn changes physique and shape. Sellers often describe it as an alternative to anabolic steroids [2][12].

Proponents point to its place in Soviet-era research on plant adaptogens, to animal and cell studies reporting anabolic or protein-synthesis effects, and to a signalling route (PI3K/AKT, and in some accounts estrogen receptor beta) that is described as different from that of androgens [1][25]. Wikipedia states that its pharmacokinetics, bioavailability and effects in humans remain to be determined [1].

Human data on turkesterone itself are small: a 2024 preliminary study of acute doses in 11 men reported no significant effects on IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism [4], and a randomised, double-blind trial of 24 students taking a turkesterone-containing supplement for four weeks reported no significant differences in body composition, handgrip strength, mood or sleep [6]. Much of the wider human literature concerns the related compound ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone), including a WADA-funded trial published in 2019 [24].

Turkesterone became a prominent topic in lifting and TRT forums in the early 2020s, where members describe it as a 'natural anabolic', add it to cutting and pre-workout stacks, and debate whether it does anything noticeable [13][15][21][22].

Sold as a dietary supplement; not an approved drug

paras: Lifters take turkesterone hoping for extra muscle growth, strength and recovery. Muscle size and strength feed directly into physique: shoulder, chest and arm fullness and overall leanness during a cut. Users describe it as an add-on to training and diet rather than a stand-alone change [13][17][23].

On T Nation, members describe trying it out of curiosity, adding it to pre-workouts alongside laxogenin and ecdysterone, using it during a cut, and taking it alongside prescribed testosterone replacement for its supposed effect on SHBG [13][14][15][16][17]. One poster describes it as a way to keep strength while dieting [23].

Reviews of ecdysterone and turkesterone describe potential in sport and nutrition and in conditions such as chronic fatigue, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, mostly on preclinical evidence [3][25]. Laboratory work has also looked at effects on fat-cell lipid accumulation [10][25].

Turkesterone has a polyhydroxylated structure on a cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene skeleton resembling cholesterol-derived steroids; Wikipedia gives its formula as C27H44O8 [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes a 27-carbon skeleton with seven hydroxyl groups [2].

It is found in Ajuga turkestanica, various Vitex species, wheat, Cyanotis arachnoidea and Rhaponticum acaule [1]. A 2020 phytochemical study of the underground parts of Rhaponticum acaule isolated 20-hydroxyecdysone and turkesterone along with three previously undescribed ecdysteroids [26]. A 2015 paper catalogued minor ecdysteroids from Ajuga turkestanica, a plant used in traditional medicine for its high ecdysteroid content [7]. Review authors list turkesterone, with 20-hydroxyecdysone, among the ecdysteroids most often found in supplements; its main commercial sources are Ajuga turkestanica, Rhaponticum carthamoides and Cyanotis arachnoidea [25].

Wikipedia says turkesterone is under laboratory investigation for anabolic effects through activation of the PI3K and AKT signalling pathways [1]. A 2024 review reports that the related 20-hydroxyecdysone does not bind the androgen receptor, so any anabolic effect would have to work through another route; it notes proposed activation of PI3K, enhanced muscle protein synthesis in animals, and a rat study in which estrogen receptor beta signalling was examined, alongside the observation that 20-hydroxyecdysone did not quickly activate mTORC1 signalling in rat muscle or liver [25]. Wikipedia's ecdysterone article describes relatively selective estrogen receptor beta activation as the proposed mechanism for that compound [24].

Forum posts repeat this framing, describing turkesterone as working through a pathway different from conventional steroids, and some claim it raises SHBG [12][16]. No published study cited here measured SHBG or androgen levels in people taking turkesterone [1][4].

Ecdysone was isolated from silkworm pupae in 1954 by Adolf Butenandt and Peter Karlson, and plant ecdysteroids were reported from the mid-1960s [25]. Turkesterone was first reported from Ajuga turkestanica in 1973 by a team in Tashkent, with structure elucidation in 1975, according to Grokipedia [2].

A 2024 review says the leuzea plant Rhaponticum carthamoides was classified as an adaptogen by Brekhman and Dardymov in 1969 and became widely used among elite athletes in Soviet and Russian sport [25]. Soviet laboratory papers compared turkesterone with the anabolic steroid nerobol: a 1978 study examined protein synthesis in mouse liver [8]. A 1997 Russian study examined phytoecdysteroids including turkesterone as erythropoiesis stimulators in laboratory animals [9].

Turkesterone moved into Western bodybuilding supplement markets in the 2010s and early 2020s. A 2021 T Nation thread describes it as 'becoming very popular (again)', citing old mouse studies that reported better results than Dianabol in mice [21].

Harris and colleagues (Muscles, 2024) gave multiple acute turkesterone conditions to 11 healthy men and sampled before ingestion, 3 hours and 24 hours after. There were no statistically significant main effects on IGF-1, resting metabolic rate or lipid and carbohydrate metabolism, although IGF-1 trended higher with turkesterone and resting metabolic rate stayed above baseline across the 3-hour window. The authors said the data do not fully support turkesterone as a potent anabolic supplement, reported favourable haemodynamic and gastrointestinal tolerability, and recommended longer studies of muscle growth across training sessions [4].

A 2025 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial gave a turkesterone-containing supplement or placebo to 24 healthy university students (12 men, 12 women, mean age 22) for four weeks without changes to diet or exercise. It measured body composition by bioimpedance, handgrip strength, mood (POMS) and sleep quality (PSQI). Change scores did not differ significantly between groups; the supplement group's mood-disturbance and sleep scores improved slightly but not significantly. The authors noted the small sample and short duration [6].

A 2021 study in 20-month-old sedentary mice gave an Ajuga turkestanica extract or 20-hydroxyecdysone orally for 28 days. It found no change in muscle or organ mass, fibre size or type, or Akt/p70S6K signalling; the authors suggested oral breakdown, advanced age and the absence of added muscle stress as possible explanations and noted that anabolic effects had been reported in young rodents and with injection or infusion [5].

A 2023 study found that Rhaponticum carthamoides extract and its ecdysteroids reduced lipid accumulation in cultured fat cells, with turkesterone among the compounds tested [10][25]. A review of Ajuga cell-culture technologies discusses producing its bioactive metabolites sustainably [27].

Because most human work uses ecdysterone rather than turkesterone, supplement discussions often borrow its results. Wikipedia reports a 2019 study by Isenmann and colleagues in Archives of Toxicology, funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency, in which participants taking ecdysterone gained more muscle mass and one-repetition bench-press strength than controls, with a dose-related effect, and an earlier 2006 study by Wilborn and colleagues in resistance-trained men that found no significant effect on body composition or training adaptations [24]. The 2024 review cites an eight-week trial in resistance-trained men that found no change in training adaptation or anabolic and catabolic markers, and notes that WADA added ecdysterone to its monitoring programme in 2020, which the authors call controversial because the compound occurs in spinach and quinoa [25]. Whether findings on ecdysterone apply to turkesterone has not been tested in published human trials [4][24].

Grokipedia says animal studies indicate low toxicity [2]. A 2024 review reports an oral LD50 above 9 g/kg in mice for ecdysterone and no obvious adverse responses in rats at high daily amounts over three months, and concludes ecdysteroids are generally considered safe in mammals, while noting most evidence is from animals or small human studies [25]. The 2024 acute-dose study reported favourable haemodynamic and gastrointestinal tolerability [4].

One T Nation poster reports that taking turkesterone at night raised blood pressure and heart rate somewhat and worsened their sleep scores, so they moved it to mornings [19]. Long-term human safety data have not been published in the sources cited here. Another poster describes concern about teenagers in a gym discussing SARMs, turkesterone, testosterone and trenbolone together [20].

Turkesterone is sold as a dietary supplement and promoted by sellers as a natural alternative to anabolic steroids; it is not an approved drug [1][2]. Wikipedia describes ecdysterone as marketed in bodybuilding supplements and not generally regulated [24]. WADA placed ecdysterone on its monitoring programme in 2020 [25].

On T Nation, members describe turkesterone as part of cutting and TRT-adjacent stacks, ask about its half-life, and compare brands [13][15][17]. Some report keeping strength during a cut, while others say they noticed no effect [23][22]. Several posters raise counterfeit or under-dosed products as a concern in the category [18].

Human studies of turkesterone itself are few: a 2024 preliminary investigation of multiple acute doses on IGF-1 and metabolic rate in 11 men [4] and a four-week randomised placebo-controlled trial of a turkesterone-containing supplement in 24 students [6]. Grokipedia describes further 2024 to 2025 randomised trials, a claim from an AI-generated source [2]. Reviews of ecdysteroids in sport are available [3][25]. Animal work includes studies of phytoecdysteroids in mice and rats [5][8][9].

lore.intro: On T Nation turkesterone is discussed as a hyped 'natural anabolic', with members split between experimenting with it and describing it as ineffective [15][22][21].

claims.claim: Turkesterone is a natural anabolic stronger than Dianabol
claims.believers: A forum thread cites old mouse studies that reported better results than Dianabol in mice and notes renewed popularity [21].
claims.experts: Reviews describe the supporting evidence for turkesterone as largely preclinical, and a small human study found no significant effect on IGF-1 or metabolic rate. [3][4]

claims.claim: It builds muscle without suppressing your natural hormones
claims.believers: A forum poster asks for an anabolic without major suppression and suggests turkesterone and ecdysterone, comparing them to low-dose Anavar and saying they kept strength during a cut [23].
claims.experts: No study cited here measured human androgen levels or suppression with turkesterone; Wikipedia lists human effects as undetermined [1].

claims.believers: A TRT forum user says turkesterone is supposed to increase SHBG a lot and plans to add it [16].
claims.experts: No published study cited here examined SHBG.

claims.claim: Turkesterone has no noticeable effect, and its promotion is driven by sellers
claims.believers: One T Nation member says turkesterone 'doesn't do anything' and that popular influencers who sell supplements describe it as great. [22]
claims.experts: A 2021 study in aged mice found no muscle effect of an Ajuga turkestanica extract, a 2025 four-week trial of a turkesterone-containing supplement found no significant differences, and the 2019 ecdysterone trial reported gains for ecdysterone specifically [5][6][24].

claims.claim: Many turkesterone products are fake or under-dosed
claims.believers: A T Nation poster warns of fakes, saying turkesterone has more of them than a related product [18].
claims.experts: No independent testing study has been published.

claims.believers: Supplement discussions borrow the WADA-funded ecdysterone trial and describe turkesterone as the more potent or 'premium' ecdysteroid [12][24].
claims.experts: Whether ecdysterone findings apply to turkesterone has not been tested in published human trials; the 2024 acute-dose study of turkesterone reported no significant IGF-1 or metabolic changes [4][24].

claims.claim: Turkesterone is safe because it is a natural plant compound
claims.believers: Sellers and some users describe it as a natural alternative with fewer side effects than anabolic steroids [2][12].
claims.experts: Reviews report low toxicity in animal studies and good tolerability in small human studies; long-term human safety data are limited, and one forum user reports higher blood pressure and heart rate when taking it at night [4][19][25].

angle.text: Lifters take turkesterone hoping for extra muscle and strength, and more muscle changes physique and shape. The signalling route is proposed from laboratory and animal work, and human data on turkesterone itself come from two small short-term studies.
